session.question: What are biomasses converted into through thermochemical decomposition?
session.answer:
Biomasses are converted through thermochemical decomposition into bio-oils, biofuels, syngas, hydrogen (H2), heat, biochar, and other value-added chemicals and bio-products. In broader thermochemical conversion systems, these outputs also include renewable liquid fuels and chemical feedstocks. (agbo2023biooilbasedepoxyresins chunk 1, rout2022sustainablevalorisationof chunk 1, liu2021thermochemicalconversionof chunk 1, shah2023developmentofsustainable chunk 1)

For lignocellulosic biomass specifically, thermochemical processing yields bio-oil among other fuels and chemicals, but the resulting bio-oil often requires upgrading because of unfavorable properties such as instability, low heating value, corrosivity, and high viscosity. (liu2021thermochemicalconversionof chunk 1)

session.context:
pqac-0482e3d4: The excerpt explains that biomass undergoes thermochemical conversion/decomposition to produce bio-oils. These bio-oils are renewable liquid fuels and can also be used as sustainable feedstocks for making bio-oil-based epoxy resins. The paper discusses thermochemical processing techniques such as organic solvent liquefaction, fast pyrolysis, and hydrothermal liquefaction used to obtain bio-oil from biomass.
From Philip Agbo, Abhijeet Mali, Dongyang Deng, and Lifeng Zhang. Bio-oil-based epoxy resins from thermochemical processing of sustainable resources: a short review. Journal of Composites Science, 2023. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/jcs7090374, doi:10.3390/jcs7090374.

pqac-26a997f7: The excerpt reviews thermochemical conversion technologies for animal manures and says that these processes can produce several valuable outputs. Specifically, thermochemical conversion of biomass/manure can generate bio-oils, syngas, hydrogen (H2), biofuels, heat, and biochar (used as a carbon-free fertilizer). The paper notes these as products of pyrolysis, combustion, supercritical gasification, and related decomposition technologies. It also mentions that bio-oils reported in the literature have calorific values of about 26–32 MJ/kg. The review emphasizes that these products make manure a potential feedstock for energy and nutrient recovery.
From Prangya Ranjan Rout, Daya Shankar Pandey, Macsen Haynes-Parry, Caitlin Briggs, Helmer Luís Cachicolo Manuel, Reddicherla Umapathi, Sanjay Mukherjee, Sagarika Panigrahi, and Mukesh Goel. Sustainable valorisation of animal manures via thermochemical conversion technologies: an inclusive review on recent trends. Waste and Biomass Valorization, 2022. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s12649-022-01916-5, doi:10.1007/s12649-022-01916-5.

pqac-ae21656e: The excerpt says lignocellulosic biomass can be converted through thermochemical processes into various value-added chemicals and biofuels, including bio-oil. It also notes that bio-oil often needs upgrading because of poor properties such as instability, low heating value, corrosivity, and high viscosity. The paper discusses emerging upgrading methods like electrocatalytic hydrogenation, atmospheric distillation, and plasma-assisted catalysis, as well as sustainability and environmental impacts of biomass conversion systems.
From Wujun Liu and Han‐Qing Yu. Thermochemical conversion of lignocellulosic biomass into mass-producible fuels: emerging technology progress and environmental sustainability evaluation. ACS Environmental Au, 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.1021/acsenvironau.1c00025, doi:10.1021/acsenvironau.1c00025.

pqac-a141f8ec: The excerpt discusses thermochemical processes for waste management and resource recovery, noting that techniques like pyrolysis, gasification, and liquefaction convert diverse waste materials into valuable products. It explicitly says thermochemical techniques convert waste into chemicals and fuels, supporting waste-to-value technologies and a circular economy. If the question is about biomass specifically, the excerpt implies biomass/waste is thermochemically decomposed into useful end products such as fuels, chemicals, and other value-added materials, though it does not give a more specific list for biomasses alone.
